title: 33. Evaluating cow-calf spatial interactions on pasture using GPS data.
content:
Abstract
Understanding cow–calf spatial interactions is essential for interpreting maternal care, calf dependency, and group dynamics in grazing systems. These interactions are dynamic and can be driven by either the cow or the calf depending on behavioral context (stationary vs. active movement). To investigate cow-calf interaction patterns on pasture, Global Positioning System (GPS) data were collected from 21 cow-calf pairs in two groups (Red and Green) at 10-min intervals from May 27 (calves aged 34±14 d) to September 13, 2025. The Red and Green groups grazed pastures averaging 8.22 and 9.57 ha, respectively. Cow and calf locations were classified as stationary or active-moving based on distances calculated from consecutive GPS points. For stationary events, mean cow-calf distance was calculated using locations centered on either the stationary cow or calf. These distances were log-transformed and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, with reference animal type (cow or calf as center), management group, and log-transformed stationary duration as fixed effects and individual animal as a random effect. For active-moving events, cow and calf locations were matched within ±5 min, and a directional alignment score was calculated to indicate movement orientation (-1 = away; +1 = toward). Cow:calf ratios were derived from counts of positive and negative alignment scores events to quantify whether cows or calves more frequently moved toward or away from their pair during movement. A lag correlation analysis of consecutive distances was conducted to assess movement synchronization (Lag -1: calf leads; Lag 0: simultaneous; Lag +1: cow leads).Our data showed that calves on average spent 84.6% of the time stationary and 15.4% active, remarkably different from cows, which spent 32.9% of the time stationary and 67.1% actively moving (p < 0.001). Under stationary conditions, reference animal type, management group, and stationary duration significantly affected mean cow-calf distance (p < 0.001). When calves were stationary, mean cow-calf distance was substantially greater, averaging 61.20±1.23 m in the Green group and 62.44±1.11 m in the Red group, compared with 22.81±0.41 m (Green) and 24.18±0.38 m (Red) when cows were stationary. In addition, mean cow–calf distance decreased with increasing stationary duration (β = -0.072, p < 0.001), regardless of reference animal type, indicating mutual cow–calf responsiveness. During active movement, cow:calf ratios were 1.47 for positive and 0.75 for negative alignment scores, indicating a stronger tendency for cows to move toward their calves than calves toward their dams. The highest correlation (r = 0.57 - 0.60) occurred at Lag 0, indicating that cows and calves tended to initiate or adjust movement simultaneously rather than exhibiting a consistent leader-follower pattern. These findings offer novel insights into cow-calf interactions in grazing systems.
